05 / Technical writing

Notes from the build.

Two project-inspired articles.

01
MACHINE LEARNING · DRAFT FOR REVIEW

From medical images to useful predictions

A practical guide to classification, segmentation, and evaluation.
Read article ↗

Medical imaging projects often combine two different questions: what is present in an image, and where is it? Classification addresses the first. Segmentation assigns labels to pixels or voxels to address the second. My medical imaging work uses VGG16 transfer learning and 3D U-Net across these tasks.

Start with the data boundary

A defensible workflow separates training, validation, and test data before fitting preprocessing steps. Where multiple images come from one patient, a patient-level split helps prevent closely related samples from appearing in both training and evaluation. This is a recommended evaluation practice; the full project protocol should document the actual split used.

Choose the model for the task

Transfer learning adapts an existing feature extractor to a new classification problem. A 3D U-Net instead works with volumetric structure to produce a segmentation mask. These models solve different problems, so choosing between them starts with defining the output the application needs.

Look beyond one score

Precision and recall expose different types of classification errors. F1 balances them, while ROC-AUC summarizes ranking behavior across thresholds. For segmentation, overlap measures such as Dice and IoU are useful additions. Report dataset size, class balance, and test conditions alongside every result.

Bring the model into a system

Inference includes loading, preprocessing, prediction, and presenting the result. Measuring the entire path gives a more useful view of latency than timing the model alone. This draft explains the project’s concepts; it does not establish clinical validation.

02
SOFTWARE ENGINEERING · DRAFT FOR REVIEW

Building a responsive gesture-controlled application

Connecting a vision model to a reliable interaction loop.
Read article ↗

A gesture recognition model becomes useful when it produces a reliable action. My hand gesture video controller combines CNN-based recognition with OpenCV. The software challenge is connecting camera input, predictions, and controls without making the interface feel unpredictable.

Separate the responsibilities

A useful design divides the application into frame capture, preprocessing, inference, decision logic, and action dispatch. Clear interfaces between these components make it easier to change a model or diagnose slow frames. This describes a recommended architecture rather than a verified inventory of the project’s implementation.

Turn predictions into deliberate actions

One uncertain frame should not repeatedly trigger a command. Confidence thresholds, agreement across a short window of frames, and a cooldown after an action are practical techniques to evaluate. Each introduces a tradeoff between responsiveness and stability.

Measure the user experience

End-to-end latency includes capture and preprocessing as well as inference. A system can have strong classification accuracy yet still feel slow or repeat actions. Test those behaviors alongside recognition quality.

Design for imperfect inputs

Lighting, backgrounds, camera position, and ambiguous gestures affect a real-time system. A clear idle state and an obvious way to pause controls can make failures easier to recover from. The resume reports 98% recognition accuracy; a complete write-up should add the test setup and dataset before interpreting that figure.
